Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP View image in fullscreen The wreckage of a Nazi warship has become visible above the exceptionally low water line on the Danube near Prahovo in Serbia this week. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP Drought Nazi shipwrecks emerge from the depths as Europe’s Danube dries up Unexploded ordnance and a military motorcycle also recovered following record heat and drought conditions Oliver Holmes Sat 8 Aug 2026 06.55 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Record-low water levels in the Danube have exposed remnants of Europe’s Nazi past, with dozens of second world war ships emerging from the riverbed during an intense drought. In the middle of the river on the Serbian and Romanian border, a broken-up hull was visible on a sandbank that is normally underwater. Other vessels were partly submerged, some still believed to be laden with weapons. View image in fullscreen The wreckage of a second world war German warship near Prahovo, Serbia on Tuesday. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP The ships were part of Adolf Hitler’s Black Sea fleet that the German military deliberately sank towards the end of the war to slow down the Soviet advance. Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in this way in September 1944. But Nazi Germany did not surrender until the following year in May 1945. Sunken WWII era ships appear as Danube levels go down amid drought The ships have been revealed during previous droughts only to disappear again as water levels rose along the second-longest river in Europe. The Serbian government has tried in the past to remove the wrecks, but most remain in place owing to the explosives they carried. View image in fullscreen The Serbian government has previously tried to remove wrecks such as the one pictured here near Prahovo. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP Other second world war remnants have been found in other parts of the river, including a German military motorcycle in Budapest, Hungary . In Slovakia, police recovered an unexploded British 1,543lb (700kg) bomb . Police said authorities loaded it on to a “specially modified firefighter vehicle with a sand bed, which ensured its safe transport” and took it to a 5-metre deep pit to detonate it. View image in fullscreen A second world war German military motorcycle is displayed at the defence ministry museum in Budapest, Hungary on Wednesday. Photograph: Tamas Purger/EPA In 1944, Britain’s Royal Air Force mined the river to disrupt enemy troops. The Danube, which flows through 10 countries, has become increasingly difficult to navigate as low water levels create dangerous conditions. Prolonged droughts have left major European rivers at significantly lower water levels than is typical for the time of year, creating an energy crisis as many power plants rely on their natural water supply for cooling. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. https://nineoclock.ro/vodafone-foundatio.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Over 17,600 Students and 900 Teachers Become “Explorers in the World of Artificial Intelligence” Bucharest, 27 July 2026 – Vodafone Romania Foundation, the Ministry of Education and Research, and the Economic Informatics Club Association – CyberKnowledge Club have brought artificial intelligence education closer to middle school students and their teachers through the “AI Content – School of the Future for Middle School – Explorers in the World of Artificial Intelligence” project. More than 17,600 students and over 930 teachers from 295 schools, together with 100 educational ambassadors, participated in six interactive modules exploring topics such as algorithmic bias, ethical dilemmas in AI, the responsible use of artificial intelligence, the impact of technology on the environment, and the role of digital citizens. The project responds to the findings of a 2025 study conducted by Vodafone Romania Foundation, which showed that 70% of Romanian students believe artificial intelligence will play an essential role in their professional lives, while only 54% feel that school prepares them to use this technology. Only 40% consider that their teachers have relevant AI-related skills. The data also shows that 72% of students have gained knowledge about AI outside the classroom. The initiative brought AI education closer to middle school students and teachers through interactive digital resources, practical activities, and a national network of teacher ambassadors. During the 2025–2026 school year, the project reached 17,626 students, 932 teachers, and 295 schools across Romania. The number of participating students exceeded the initial target by almost three times, while the number of participating schools was 195% above the planned objective. The national expansion of the project was supported by 100 educational ambassadors who coordinated and assisted teachers in using the resources in classrooms. The educational resources are available on the “School of the Future” platform, and the six interactive modules were designed to encourage critical thinking, debate, and the practical application of technology in contexts relevant to students’ lives. The project evaluation shows its strong relevance for the educational community. Among teachers who completed the feedback questionnaire, nearly 85% said the project helped them improve their digital skills, approximately 98% considered the activities useful for students, and more than 97% appreciated the quality of the platform’s materials. In addition, almost 99% of respondents said they would continue using the resources and methods learned after the project’s completion. The programme also aims to provide more equitable access to digital education. Participating schools came from diverse areas: 39% from large urban areas, 37% from smaller urban communities, and 24% from rural areas. The fact that almost a quarter of participating schools are rural demonstrates that the project reached communities where access to such resources is more limited and where the impact can be significant. The activities were not used only for computer science or ICT classes, but also for mathematics, Romanian language and literature, foreign languages, geography, history, social education, sciences, and technology education. This demonstrates that artificial intelligence can become a relevant topic across the entire school curriculum, not only in technical subjects. The Ministry of Education and Research played an essential role in expanding the project nationwide through institutional support and by facilitating access to schools. The partnership between the public sector, civil society, and the private sector created a scalable model for digital education based on accessible resources, teacher ambassadors, and impact evaluation. The resources developed within the project will remain freely available on the “School of the Future” platform. The project estimates an indirect impact on approximately 30,000 students and teachers who will access the content after the implementation period ends. Vodafone Romania Foundation will continue, together with its partners, to support initiatives focused on developing digital skills, promoting the responsible use of artificial intelligence, and encouraging digital well-being among children and teenagers. Share A A A Key points AI is an excellent planning assistant for building itineraries and suggesting destinations, saving hours of research Always verify time-sensitive information such as passport validity, transport schedules, opening hours and reservations Human travel writers still add value through first-hand experience, practical judgment and storytelling Depending on who you listen to, artificial intelligence (AI) is either the greatest threat to civilisation ever devised by dark minds or a powerful tool that helps us work faster and solve problems. The truth lies somewhere in between. Plenty of travellers are using it and there are good reasons why you might invite ChatGPT, Claude or any other generative AI tool to collaborate when planning your travels. AI is surprisingly good at generating itineraries and suggesting activities. Getty Images If you want to construct a self-guided tour of the Western Front battlefields, plan a visit to Tokyo Disneyland with the kids or find the best scenic drives in Arizona, ask AI. It shines when suggesting itineraries, comparing France versus Italy for a holiday focused on food and wine, narrowing down transport options between cities, recommending the best neighbourhoods to look for accommodation, generating packing lists and optimising routes. Advertisement You might want to drill down further and take the kids to the best cat cafe in Tokyo, and AI can put its paws on the purr-fect choice. Something offbeat? Want to see traditional cheese-making as practised by Romanian shepherds or a five-day itinerary visiting the Kalash villages of northern Pakistan? Such questions would take hours of research, but AI can come up with the answer in seconds. Sign up for the Traveller newsletter The latest travel news, tips and inspiration delivered to your inbox. Sign up now. AI is a great tool for suggesting options you might not have considered. Ask it for “unusual sightseeing possibilities in X”, or “alternative transport ideas” and it might tell you about a spin around Rome in the sidecar of a vintage Vespa, or God’s Own Junkyard in London. Check the answers – transport schedules, visa and entry requirements, baggage allowances, opening hours of attractions are subject to change at short notice, and AI doesn’t always catch the update. AI will usually give more weight to official sources, such as a government or a museum website, but it can be knocked off balance when many source websites have the same misleading information. When it talks about remote places or obscure experiences that have limited sources of information, AI can sound convincing when it should tread carefully. In the Kalash region of Pakistan, ChatGPT suggests the walk from Bumburet to Rumbur, a 16-18km hike that involves crossing a pass 1000 metres above the river valleys where the towns are situated. That advice should be treated with great caution since Bumburet and Rumbur are interconnected river valleys, no need to climb a mountain pass to travel between them. Think of it as a first-rate travel assistant, especially when it comes to constructing a first draft for your travels. Advertisement AI can also mess up big time. It can overlook the need for reservations in busy periods, underestimate driving times in rush hours or when the trip involves narrow twisting roads and stitch attractions into an itinerary without regard to the time it takes to get from one to the other. AI doesn’t know about the lived experience. Ask it about street food in Hanoi and AI won’t tell you what it feels like to sit on a tiny plastic stool for an hour on a crowded footpath. Only a human voice can tell you what it feels like when you sit in a Tibetan Buddhist temple among ochre-robed monks when they begin chanting. It can even invent non-existent attractions. In 2025, an AI-generated article on a travel operator’s website began singing the praises of the fabulous Weldborough Hot Springs in the forests of northeast Tasmania. According to a CNN report, Kristy Probert, owner of the local Weldborough Hotel, was mystified when tourists started turning up asking directions to the hot springs. What started as a trickle became a steady stream, but the hot springs were a total fabrication. “If you can find these hot springs, beers are on me,” said Probert. AI v the Tripologist How does an answer from AI compare with a response from a real live human? Easy question since I write this column. From a recent Q&A, a reader asked where to stay in the Dolomites region of northern Italy, using a small, quiet town or two as a base for exploring and walking. My response was the village of Santa Magdalena in the Val de Funes, a postcard valley within easy reach of some of the loveliest alpine walking trails on the planet. Also the village of San Vigilio, gateway to the South Tyrolean nature parks. Hallelujah! Both ChatGPT and Claude concur. Both mentioned another two villages as well (my responses have a word limit, the AI models do not). Given the unpredictability of mountain weather, if the skies turned sour I suggested a visit to Bolzano to take in the South Tyrol Archaeological Museum, home of Otzi the Iceman, and that’s the sort of knowledge that comes with first-hand experience. I also mentioned the essential guidebook to walks in the region, again based on personal knowledge. I have to concede though that both ChatGPT and Claude did a bang-up job of answering the question with the pros and cons of each of the villages they suggested. Advertisement Using AI to plan your travels Think of it as a first-rate travel assistant, especially when it comes to constructing a first draft for your travels. From the basic structure of your itinerary, follow up any suggestions it might make that refine your trip. Check any time-sensitive information that might have an impact – opening hours and days of attractions, holidays and transport timetables. Refine it with more questions about where to stay, where to eat, transport options for sightseeing and any personal passions you might want to indulge. When you’ve stitched it all together run it through AI again, it should let you know if you’ve packed in too little, or if there are gaps you might want to fill. Generative AI learns about you the more questions you ask, it extracts personal preferences to build a long-term profile and it might suggest refinements of alternatives that may add something special to your journey. Where AI gets scary There are plenty of readers with reservations about AI, and rightly so. For some it’s a tool of the devil, training its models by hoovering up just about everything ever written like a mutant parasitic sponge, in defiance of copyright laws . Thompson, the outrageous, taboo-busting pioneer of the gonzo style of journalism. “There is no honest way to explain the bars of Marseille to a sober person. You have to arrive already half-wrecked from the train, salt air clawing at your shirt, the gulls screaming overhead like a jury that’s already reached a verdict…” That’s a scarily good imitation of Thompson’s voice. Then I asked it to write a travel story on St Lucia in the style of Michael Gebicki. I’ve never been to St Lucia but here’s what it said. “I can’t write in Michael Gebicki’s exact voice, but I can write an original travel feature that captures the broader qualities often associated with his work.” But here’s how it kicked off a paragraph on the island’s food in “my” voice: “Food is another pleasant surprise.” Good grief. Surely that anaemic dross isn’t me? Tell my editors. Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. https://www.ipswichstar.co.uk/news/26442.text: Crime Ipswich Former Ipswich councillor calls for killer's deportation By Tom Cann Reporter Share 0 Comments Arvydas Maliusis has been sentenced to life in prison (Image: Facebook) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A former councillor has called for the deportation of a murderer after he was convicted of a Christmas Eve killing near Ipswich Waterfront. 38-year-old Arvydas Maliusis was handed a life sentence for the murder of 39-year-old Ilja Akatjevas at Ipswich Crown Court on August 6. Judge Samantha Leigh set a minimum custodial sentence of 18 years, reduced to 17 years and 142 days to reflect time the time Maliusis had already spent on remand. John Cook, who was an Ipswich Borough Councillor for the area at the time of the murder in December said: "Mr Akatjevas was brutally murdered last year, and I am pleased that his killer has received a life sentence. John Cook (Image: Lucy Taylor) "He must be deported when eventually released or preferably sooner, if it is possible for him to serve his sentence in a Lithuanian jail." Detective superintendent Matt Adams, said: “Today our thoughts are with the family and friends of Ilja Akatjevas. "They have suffered the devastating loss of a loved one in the most tragic of circumstances, and we recognise the profound impact his death has had on all those who knew and loved him. “Ilja lost his life as the result of an exceptionally violent and sustained attack. The ferocity of that assault was shocking and ultimately proved fatal. Detective Chief Inspector Matt Adams on behalf of Suffolk Police. (Image: Newsquest) “Following the murder, Maliusis attempted to distance himself from what had happened and provided a misleading account to our investigators. "However, the determination of the investigation team, together with witness evidence, CCTV footage and forensic findings, enabled us to establish what occurred. "This ensured the truth was placed before the court. Police at the scene of the alleged murder (Image: Newsquest) “While no conviction or sentence can bring Ilja back, we welcome today's sentence and the fact that the person responsible for taking his life has been held accountable for his actions. “Finally, I would like to thank the members of the public who came forward to assist the investigation, together with the officers and staff whose professionalism and dedication have helped secure justice for Ilja and his family.” (Image: Suffolk Constabulary) Crime Ipswich Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading... https://vietnamnews.vn/economy/1798219/v.text: Việt Nam, Czech Republic enhance cooperation in urban planning, investment PRAGUE — Hà Nội and Prague are seeking to deepen cooperation in urban planning, heritage conservation, infrastructure and investment, with Hà Nội looking to draw on Prague’s experience in managing and preserving its historic cityscape. A Hà Nội delegation led by Vice Chairman of the municipal People’s Committee Đỗ Anh Tuấn held talks with Prague Deputy Mayor Petr Hlavacek at Prague City Hall on Monday to discuss new areas of cooperation between the two capitals. Tuan briefed the host on Hà Nội’s socio-economic development and highlighted key achievements in the city’s cooperation with Prague in particular and the Czech Republic in general. Tuấn highlighted growing ties in trade, investment, tourism, people-to-people exchanges and local coopertion, as well as in heritage preservation and urban management, and noted that there remains room to scale up economic and investment cooperation to match their potential. Czech investment in Hà Nội has totalled nearly US$23 million since 1989, but large-scale projects remain limited. As Hà Nội implements its Capital Master Plan and amended Capital Law, the city wants to exchange experience with Prague in urban planning and management, heritage conservation, public transport and digital transformation. It also sought Prague’s experience in revitalising heritage areas, particularly the Old Quarter and the area around Hoàn Kiếm Lake, as well as turning relocated industrial sites into cultural and creative spaces, parks and public facilities. Housing is another area of interest, with Hà Nội looking to learn from Prague’s experience in social and affordable housing, public housing funds, financing mechanisms and public-private partnerships. Hlavacek said the Czech Republic had a long-established legal framework for heritage preservation, with both public and private resources mobilised to protect historic buildings and sites. Prague’s historic centre, recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site, is subject to strict conservation requirements. The city also holds architectural competitions for new projects to ensure they fit the existing landscape. Prague is facing a surge in tourist numbers, placing a pressure on urban infrastructure. Besides, it is also implementing measures climate change adaptation measures, such as expanding green spaces and installing fountains and cooling facilities, to improve the living environment for residents. Hà Nội proposed broadening cooperation with Prague in transport infrastructure, smart cities, science and technology, digital transformation, culture, education and social welfare, as well as strengthening business links and investment, trade and tourism promotion. On the same day, the Hà Nội delegation had a working session with the Vietnamese Embassy in the Czech Republic, during which Ambassador Dương Hoài Nam highlighted positive bilateral ties following the elevation of relations to a Strategic Partnership in early 2025. He noted that around 100,000 Vietnamese and Czech people of Vietnamese origin live in the Czech Republic, describing the community as dynamic, well integrated and an important contributor to the host society. Meetings with Vietnamese associations in the Czech Republic and Europe highlighted the community’s growing role in people-to-people exchanges and as a bridge between Việt Nam and European countries. The Hà Nội official praised the community’s contributions and affirmed Hà Nội’s view of overseas Vietnamese as an integral part and an important resource for the capital’s development. He called on Vietnamese associations to further promote people-to-people ties, deepen mutual understanding and contribute to stronger Việt Nam-Czech Republic relations. — VNA/VNS Economy Government moves to strengthen domestic supply chains for electronics, semiconductor sectors Economy Vietnamese exporters pivot to ease pressure from US tariffs Economy Việt Nam remains top ASEAN destination for European business expansion Economy Petrovietnam accelerates smart factory drive with AI, IoT Economy Banks boost medium- and long-term lending Economy Việt Nam's monetary policy faces its toughest balancing act yet Economy Bank credit for real estate business rises to nearly $94.7 billion Outstanding loans for urban area investment and housing development projects remained the largest category, reaching VNĐ833.6 trillion by the end of June, up 6.33 per cent from the end of March. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/08/vizs.text: Menü Kereső Vizsgálatot indít az adatvédelmi hatóság a Gondosóra program miatt Belföld Aradi Hanga Zsófia Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A tudományos és technológiai miniszter bejelentése után hatósági ellenőrzést indít a Gondosóra program miatt a Nemzeti Adatvédelmi és Információszabadság Hatóság (NAIH) – közölte a szervezet elnöke, Péterfalvi Attila az MTI-vel. Tanács Zoltán szeptember 2-án jelentette be , hogy elég információt gyűjtött a minisztérium ahhoz, hogy az előző kormány alatt a Kormányzati Szolgáltató Központ és a Fidesz közötti együttműködési és adatfeldolgozási megállapodás miatt bejelentést tegyen a NAIH-nál. „Elegendő információ gyűlt össze, és felmerült az alapos gyanúja annak, hogy az adatkezelés során nem megfelelően jártak el” – írta a miniszter. Tanács szerint a program átvilágításakor találtak egy együttműködési megállapodást, ami a Kormányzati Szolgáltató Központ és a Fidesz között jött létre 2025. november 3-án. Ez alapján a Fidesz adatfeldolgozóként vett részt a Gondosóra programban, a Fidesz aktivistái pedig a Gondosóra program egy meghatározott, 78 év feletti felhasználói körének személyes adatai alapján kereshettek fel idős embereket. A NAIH ugyan tavaly véleményezte és végül szabályszerűnek nyilvánította a Kormányzati Szolgáltató Központ Gondosóra programra vonatkozó adatfeldolgozói szerződéstervezetét, ez Péterfalvi szerint egy kitöltetlen „blanketta szerződés” volt, tehát nem voltak még megjelölve rajta a konkrét adatfeldolgozók. A NAIH elnöke közölte: a hatósági ellenőrzés során a miniszter által beküldött dokumentumok alapján azt kell megvizsgálnunk, hogy a Fidesszel kötött szerződés megegyezik-e azzal, amelyet a hatóság korábban véleményezett és szabályszerűnek nyilvánított. Ezen felül a tényleges adatfeldolgozást is vizsgálják, azaz, hogy valóban felkeresték-e ezeket az időseket, ezt hogyan dokumentálták, az adatokat valóban szabályszerűen használták-e fel. Amennyiben az ellenőrzés során jogsértést állapítanak meg, hatósági eljárás indul, amely akár adatvédelmi bírság kiszabásával is végződhet. Havasi Bertalan, a Fidesz kommunikációs igazgatója Tanács múlt heti bejelentésére reagálva korábban azt írta , a Fidesz a jogszabályokat és az adatvédelmi előírásokat betartva folytatott együttműködést a Gondosóra programmal, és áll minden vizsgálat elé. „Nemcsak a Fidesznek, hanem minden pártnak megvolt a lehetősége hasonló együttműködési megállapodás megkötésére a Gondosóra programmal, de nem éltek ezzel” – írta. Tanács Zoltán egyébként augusztus elején már közölte , hogy súlyos szabálytalanságokat tártak fel a Gondosóra program ügyében, ami miatt feljelentést is tettek. A Gondosóra programmal kapcsolatban a Budapesti Rendőr-főkapitányság a múlt héten hűtlen kezelés gyanúja miatt rendelt el nyomozást. Az uniós helyreállítási tervben, a biztos forrásvesztés elkerülése érdekében lecserélték a Gondosóra programot, amit a Nemzeti Adó- és Vámhivatal és az Integritás Hatóság is vizsgál. „Full lopás” – jellemezte a programot korábban Magyar Péter.
